text_blocks.snippet: New treatments for pulmonary fibrosis are actively being researched, with some showing promising results in clinical trials. While currently available treatments like nintedanib and pirfenidone can slow disease progression, they don't stop or reverse lung scarring. Emerging therapies include stem cell therapy, immunomodulatory agents, and drugs targeting specific pathways involved in fibrosis.

list.title: Pirfenidone and Nintedanib:
list.snippet: These are the two FDA-approved medications currently used to manage IPF. They slow down the progression of lung scarring but don't stop it entirely.

list.title: Antifibrotic agents and Corticosteroids:
list.snippet: These are used in some cases, particularly for post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis.

list.title: Symptom Management:
list.snippet: Medications like opioids and anti-acids are used to manage cough and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which can worsen symptoms.
Stem Cell Therapy: This therapy aims to repair damaged lung tissue and modulate the immune response, potentially reversing fibrosis.
Immunomodulatory Agents: These aim to reduce inflammation and fibrosis in the lungs.
Novel Pharmacological Targets: Research is exploring new targets for drug development, such as:
PDE4B inhibitors: These target specific pathways involved in fibrosis.
Pamrevlumab: An antibody that targets CTGF, a protein involved in fibrosis.
PBI 4050: A drug that targets GPR40 and GPR82.
PLN 74809: An inhibitor of integrins αvβ6 and αvβ1.
Saracatinib: An experimental anticancer drug that has shown promise in preclinical studies for reversing the disease signature of IPF, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Vixarelimab and BMS-986278: UCSF is exploring their effects on patients in clinical trials.
DWN12088 and Ifetroban: UCSF is also evaluating the safety and effectiveness of these drugs.
